chunks: "Each one has one job. The inductor is the energy store.
When the switch is on it charges from the input, and when the switch turns off its current has to keep flowing, so it pushes that current into the output at a voltage higher than the input.
Without it there's no step-up. Its value sets the ripple current, and I need to check its saturation current against the peak current. The diode is the one-way valve.
When the switch is off it lets the inductor current flow to the output.
When the switch turns on, SW goes to ground and the diode blocks, so the output capacitor can't discharge back through the switch.
Without it the output would be shorted to ground every cycle.
I'd pick a Schottky for low forward drop and make sure its reverse voltage and peak current ratings cover V out and the inductor peak. The capacitor holds up the output.
During the on-time nothing is coming from the inductor, so the capacitor alone supplies the load, and it absorbs the pulsed diode current during the off-time.
It sets the output ripple, and what matters is capacitance, ESR and ripple current rating. And for ceramics, derating under DC bias."
